facts.text: The prelude opens on very soft, very high strings, the frail heroine. Then the love theme, on lower strings.
evidence: The prelude to the opera begins with very soft, very high strings depicting the frail heroine, followed by the main love theme of the opera, which is then played on lower strings

facts.text: Curtain up, and lively dance tunes take over. Waltz rhythms run through all of Act I: Paris, in three-quarter time.
evidence: This delicate atmosphere is altered on curtain rise by lively dance tunes in the orchestra.
waltz rhythms pervade the first act of the opera, creating a Parisian atmosphere

facts.text: La traviata is the only one of Verdi’s many operas set entirely indoors.
evidence: La traviata is the only one of Verdi's many operas to be set entirely indoors.

facts.text: The Brindisi: a drinking song in B-flat major, in a lilting 3/8, marked Allegretto.
evidence: The song is a brindisi
The piece is written in B-flat major, its time signature is 3/8, and the tempo is marked Allegretto

facts.text: That offstage band? Verdi sketched its waltzes like a piano score and left the scoring to the bandmaster.
evidence: an offstage band plays a series of waltzes
Verdi did not fully orchestrate the parts of the on-stage band, but rather composed it in the style of a piano reduction, leaving the actual realization to the person in charge of the band.

facts.text: “Sempre libera” is all feverish ornamentation. Savor it: Violetta never needs coloratura again after Act I.
evidence: full of vocal decoration and feverish ornamentation as she swears to stay free ("Sempre libera")
These coloratura effects are not required for the character after the first act.

facts.text: Verdi wanted a modern-dress setting. La Fenice insisted on the past: “c. 1700”.
evidence: Piave and Verdi wanted to follow Dumas in giving the opera a contemporary setting, but the authorities at La Fenice insisted that it be set in the past, "c. 1700".

facts.text: Dumas fils turned his 1848 novel into the 1852 play La Dame aux camélias. Verdi’s opera followed in 1853.
evidence: It is based on La Dame aux camélias (1852), a play by Alexandre Dumas fils, which he adapted from his own 1848 novel.
It was first performed on 6 March 1853

facts.text: The great Germont–Violetta duet begins: many sections, the music turning with every shift in the drama.
evidence: The lengthy and crucial duet between the elder Germont and Violetta in act 2 is multi-sectioned with the music following the changing dramatic situation.

facts.text: Violetta’s music has traveled: hectic coloratura in Act I, drama in Act II, and now a spiritual quality.
evidence: from the hectic, almost hysterical coloratura of the first act, to the more dramatic passages of the second, and the spiritual quality of her music as she dies in act 3
